newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Soldiers on alert as protests grip Albania.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers on alert as protests grip Albania.

text.p: Soldiers were deployed in the Albanian capital Tirana on Sunday after demonstrators fought with riot police there and torched buildings in towns in the south in growing protests over collapsing savings schemes.

Thousands of angry demonstrators, fearing they may lose all their cash invested in pyramid savings funds, clashed with ranks of police who lashed out with batons to try to disperse a crowd of around 30,000 in central Tirana.

Police fired their pistols in the air over the ear-shattering din of shouts and screams as a hard core of around 3,000 protesters tried to advance towards parliament, hurling stones through windows and glass doors of buildings bordering central Skanderbeg Square.
Albanian state media reported disturbances in 13 other towns in the impoverished Balkan state.
Violence erupted in Vlore, 150 km (100 miles) south of the capital, when protesters forced their way past police cordons and set fire to the town hall.

Administrative buildings of the state-owned oil company Albpetrol were engulfed in flames in the southern town of Patos, a company official speaking from the neighbouring town of Fier, 115 km (80 miles) south of Tirana, told Reuters.

President Sali Berisha summoned an emergency meeting of his ruling right-wing Democratic Party later on Sunday to discuss the escalating crisis, also attended by Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and other cabinet members.
Soldiers armed with machine-guns were positioned around government buildings, including the interior and defence ministries.
Parliament met in urgent session, the first time the assembly has convened on Sunday since Berisha's party ousted former communists in a landslide election in 1992.
"Down with Berisha!", "Down with Meksi!", "Down with the thieves!", demonstrators in Tirana shouted before the clashes.

The crowd later dispersed. One of Tirana's main hospitals said it had treated seven demonstrators and seven police officers. Three protesters remained in hospital, one of them in intensive care, a duty doctor told Reuters.
The Tirana demonstration was called by opposition party leaders sensing the political tide was turning against the ruling Democrats over their handling of the investment schemes.
Ten national savings schemes were in operation in Albania, and protests began to spread two weeks ago when two of them were declared bankrupt, infuriating investors who fear being left penniless.
Some Albanians, unused to the ways of a free market, sold their homes, farms and livestock to pour all their money into the investment schemes.
Neritan Ceka, leader of the opposition Democratic Alliance, said opposition parties were urging demonstrators to remain peaceful but warned the authorities not to use force.
"If they dare to arrest us during the night, we will be forced to attack the police very hard," Ceka told reporters.

The Socialist Party, heirs to the former communists, said it was preparing a statement calling for the resignation of Meksi's government and demanding an interim government made up of experts ahead of a fresh general election.
State television reported protests across southern Albania in Fier, Korce, Fushe Kruje, Berat, Memaliaj, Sarande, Mallakaster, Gramsh, Skrapar, Patos and Polican.
There was renewed trouble on Sunday in Lushnje, where an angry crowd on Saturday attacked Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu, who is also Democratic Party chairman.

Shehu, who had travelled to Lushnje to try to calm the situation, was beaten on the head and was forced to flee into the locker rooms of the local soccer stadium, where he remained with his bodyguards. He stole away late at night in an unmarked car during a power cut.
